title: SOC tells PUCSL, energy utilities to end silo mentality | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 05:13
-     - 29

SOC on Infrastructure and Strategic Development Chairman and SJB MP S.M. Marikkar

Parliament’s Sectoral Oversight Committee (SOC) on Infrastructure and Strategic Development Chairman and SJB MP S.M. Marikkar this week called on the Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka (PUCSL) and energy utilities, including the National System Operator (NSO), to stop operating in silos and work together to prevent a repeat of last Saturday’s island-wide blackout.

Marikkar also urged the regulator and utilities to engage consumers and the public on the need to balance the grid, including why rooftop solar systems must be switched off when necessary. While acknowledging that solar energy delivers cheaper per-unit costs, he said the public was unaware of the complexities of keeping the grid balanced. He called for a final report on the blackout to ensure it does not happen again.

Initial investigations presented to the Committee showed that Unit 1 of the Norochcholai coal power plant, generating 187 MW, dropped to 5 MW. The plant’s three units together were supplying 529 MW, while solar was feeding 1,700 MW into the grid. The resulting imbalance triggered a total system failure at 11.43 a.m. on 17 October. A technical evaluation of why the grid failed is ongoing.

The grid was rebuilt in stages, with the Biyagama grid substation receiving the first supply from hydropower plants, and essential feeders received electricity before 4 p.m. Officials told the Committee that the NSO had requested rooftop solar owners to switch off their systems to stabilise the grid, but many did not respond. Rooftop systems needed to respond just as other power plants do, they said.

The request is not arbitrary. During restoration, the system operator brings generation and demand back online in carefully matched blocks. Rooftop systems reconnect automatically once their feeder is energised, injecting power the operator can neither see nor control, which can push a fragile, partially restored grid out of balance and risk another collapse.

PUCSL also showed how electricity consumption has changed. Peak demand, traditionally after dark when lights come on and households run appliances, now occurs during the day, reflecting heightened commercial activity, a natural shift for an emerging economy. The shift has implications for capacity expansion plans and tariffs, which have been built around an evening peak. 

The blackout over the weekend was the second island-wide grid failure in under two years. On 9 February, 2025, the grid collapsed on a low-demand Sunday after a fault at the Panadura grid substation, and supply took more than six hours to restore. 

The then Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB appointed an expert committee attributed that blackout mainly to low system inertia caused by an unusually high solar contribution, as the conventional plants that stabilise the grid were running at minimal levels. The PUCSL rejected the report and held its own public hearing in August 2025. As recently as August this year, the Electricity Consumers’ Association claimed no proper investigation had been carried out.

title: Norochcholai restart a multi-day process, says  Energy Ministry | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 05:13
-     - 17

The Ministry of Energy has defended the time taken to bring the Lakvijaya Power Plant in Norochcholai back online after shutdowns, saying a safe restart of the coal-fired facility can take several days.

Responding to public concern over the delays, the Ministry said the plant’s boiler and its metal components operate at extremely high temperatures and cannot be cooled or reheated abruptly, as uneven expansion and contraction would damage them. The turbines face a similar constraint, needing to reach the required temperature, pressure and operating conditions before running, with any shortcut risking costly machinery.

Each restart therefore follows a fixed sequence. Engineers first establish what caused the shutdown and examine pumps, valves, electrical systems and safety equipment, fixing any faults found. Only then is the boiler slowly brought up to temperature and pressure, with steam fed to the turbine in controlled stages to build up speed. Finally, the generator is synchronised with the national grid and output raised incrementally.

How long this takes varies with the circumstances of the shutdown, the condition of the equipment and the nature of the fault, the Ministry said, noting that while a major malfunction or prolonged outage would lengthen recovery, not every shutdown requires several days.

title: JAAF backs PUCSL call for simple, cost-based power wheeling tariff | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 05:12
-     - 12

The Joint Apparel Association Forum (JAAF) yesterday welcomed the Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka’s (PUCSL) call for a simple, transparent and cost-based wheeling tariff, describing it as a practical step towards more competitive energy for Sri Lanka’s industries.

Speaking at the Sri Lanka Economic and Investment Summit 2026, PUCSL Director General and CEO Damitha Kumarasinghe said the tariff should be easy to understand, affordable enough to encourage investment, and fair to transmission and distribution companies, covering their costs with a reasonable return. He said discussions are at an early stage and depend on the Gazetting of the relevant legal provisions.

Wheeling allows electricity generated by one party to be carried through the national grid to another customer for a regulated charge. For manufacturers, it could mean more flexibility in how they buy power and the ability to agree supply terms directly with generators.

Kumarasinghe also said investors should be able to secure electricity before committing capital, instead of waiting for generation capacity to follow an investment decision. He estimated that 15% to 20% of electricity could eventually be traded through a market mechanism, and said both wheeling and market-based trading need to be developed.

Issuing a statement, JAAF said the wider energy policy picture matters just as much. Open access and power wheeling regulations are moving towards being fast-tracked, and stronger incentives for battery storage are set to sit alongside them. Together, these steps could give manufacturers power options that are more dependable and more sustainable.

JAAF encourages the prompt Gazetting of the legal provisions needed to move the tariff forward, and a simple, transparent, cost-based tariff that does not discourage investment. It also calls for consultation with industry, including exporters and other energy users, before the tariff is finalised, and for fair access for businesses of all sizes, including small and medium manufacturers.

JAAF said it looks forward to working with PUCSL, the Ministry and other stakeholders so that wheeling and electricity market reforms deliver certainty for investors and competitive energy for exporters.

title: India’s PVR Inox targets high single-digit cinema footprint in Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 05:10
-     - 31

PVR Inox CEO of the Luxury Collection and Innovation and PVR Lanka Director Renaud Palliere - Pic by Lasantha Kumara

By Charumini de Silva

India’s cinema giant, PVR Inox is stepping up its expansion plans in Sri Lanka, with Jaffna emerging as its likely next location and a high single-digit number of cinema properties targeted over the next three to five years, as it seeks to tap demand beyond Colombo.

The company, which has operated in Sri Lanka for six years, is exploring opportunities in the South, Greater Colombo, Kandy and other regions, with expansion expected to combine direct investments with asset-light and franchise models involving local investors and property developers.

“Sri Lanka had become a priority for expansion following the performance of its existing operation,” PVR Inox CEO of the Luxury Collection and Innovation and PVR Lanka Director Renaud Palliere told the Daily FT.

“We feel it is absolutely time to expand the brand and give other communities and catchments in Sri Lanka the PVR experience,” he said.

Palliere said Jaffna was the most likely next destination, noting the strong response to Tamil films among audiences travelling from the northern city. The company is looking at a short-term timeline of around four months, although the investment value and final arrangements have yet to be disclosed.

Unlike its nine-screen flagship complex at One Galle Face mall, future locations are expected to feature four or five screens, with a mix of auditorium formats and seating options, including premium large-format experiences.

He said the company is also open to partnerships with local investors and real estate developers, allowing the PVR brand to be introduced into existing or planned properties without requiring the group to own every asset.

Palliere said the company’s initial investment of $ 7 million was expected to be fully recovered by the end of the current financial year or the beginning of the next, after accounting for nearly two years of closure during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Subsequent investment in upgrading the cinema experience, including the introduction of Dolby Atmos, was smaller and recovered within months, he said.

“We realised there is demand and keen interest in cinema-going in this market at a different price point, as long as the experience is differentiated,” he stressed.

Palliere added that the size of Sri Lanka’s market relative to India did not undermine its growth potential, pointing to untapped geographical markets and the company’s ability to meet its performance targets.

Noting that PVR is still at an early stage of securing local financial partners, Palliere said there was already interest. “The company sees opportunities to increase the value and rental yields of commercial properties by incorporating branded cinema facilities,” he added.

He said the group is not currently considering acquisitions of other cinema operators in Sri Lanka, as organic expansion through partnerships and franchise arrangements remaining the priority.

The expansion strategy will also be shaped by the availability of suitable retail and entertainment developments. Palliere cited the possibility of a larger complex in Galle and Kandy, while stressing that the nine-screen Colombo property was an exception rather than the template for every new location.

Palliere said Tamil and Hollywood films remained among the strongest audience draws in Sri Lanka, followed by Hindi films, while Sinhala films were attracting increasing box-office attention.

Although PVR does not intend to finance or produce films in Sri Lanka or India, he said stronger box-office performance by local productions could help attract funding and improve recognition of the industry’s output.

He also welcomed the competition as a positive sign for the market. “There is one competitor clearly picking up properties and expanding, which validates our thesis that there is an opportunity in this market,” he said, adding that a market where customers have choice keeps everybody on their toes and pushes to improve their offering.  

He described the competitive environment as healthy, noting that the two companies also worked together in film distribution.

Palliere cited occupancy of around 40% as evidence of continued audience demand, while emphasising the appeal of watching films on a large screen.

PVR Lanka currently participates in the Shangri-La ecosystem’s loyalty program and does not yet operate a standalone national program. However, Palliere said credit card offers and other initiatives were being processed, with broader partnerships likely to become more relevant as the company expands beyond a single property.

The planned expansion, he said, would allow PVR to build a wider customer base and develop loyalty initiatives suited to a multi-location operation.

He also said they hope to bring South Indian actors down for future movie premieres, believing their presence will draw massive crowds to theaters.

title: IMF sees SL tapping global Bond market for $ 3 b by 2028 | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 05:07
-     - 29

Finance and Planning Deputy Minister Dr. Anil Jayantha Fernando

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) projects Sri Lanka will raise $ 3 billion through International Sovereign Bond issues by 2028, but the Government will decide whether to tap global markets, Finance and Planning Deputy Minister Dr. Anil Jayantha Fernando told Parliament yesterday.

The IMF’s combined fifth and sixth review staff report under the Extended Fund Facility (EFF) makes no projection for a sovereign bond issue in 2026, but assumes $ 1.5 billion each in 2027 and 2028, and none in 2029. “These assumptions about borrowing through sovereign bonds are made by the IMF and should not be considered as projections of Sri Lankan authorities,” Dr. Fernando said, adding that the Government will decide periodically whether to issue sovereign bonds after assessing the situation.

Alongside future borrowing, the Government faces short-term foreign currency obligations. Outstanding currency swaps, agreements to exchange currencies now and reverse the trade later, amounted to $ 4.1 billion at end-May 2026, comprising $ 1.8 billion international and $ 2.3 billion domestic. Only about $ 83 million of the domestic swaps mature beyond one year, with the rest due within 12 months. Domestic swaps peaked at $ 2.7 billion in August 2016. There are no outstanding forwards or other short-term foreign currency liabilities with domestic banks, Dr. Fernando said.

Meanwhile, the Public Debt Management Office (PDMO) is strengthening the regulatory framework for liability management operations, which aim to reduce financing, interest rate and currency risks in the Government’s debt portfolio, and is assessing opportune market conditions and available instruments. Dr. Fernando declined to detail specific operations or strategies, describing them as highly sensitive information.

The bond assumptions also feed into the IMF’s projected path for gross official reserves, which Dr. Fernando stressed is not a program target. “The gross official reserves is not a target set out under the IMF EFF program. The relevant program target is the program net international reserves as defined in the published IMF EFF documents,” he said. The program net international reserves (NIR) for the year-end is $ 944 million. Gross reserves count all foreign assets held by the Central Bank, while NIR deducts short-term foreign currency liabilities, giving a narrower measure of reserves the country actually owns.

Gross official reserves have risen from $ 1.85 billion in June 2022 to $ 3.72 billion in June 2023, $ 5.65 billion in June 2024 and $ 6.12 billion in December 2024. They climbed to $ 6.84 billion in December 2025, dipped to $ 6.46 billion, or 3.2 months of imports, in June 2026, and recovered to $ 6.9 billion, or 3.4 months of imports, in August.

The build-up has been driven by Central Bank purchases of foreign exchange from the market, which have slowed. Net purchases fell from $ 1.76 billion in the six months to June 2024 to $ 1.08 billion in the second half of 2024, $ 1.01 billion and $ 0.98 billion in the two halves of 2025, and $ 0.56 billion in the six months to June 2026.

Gross reserves include the People’s Bank of China swap facility. Other than that swap and a marginal amount of encumbered foreign currency balances, reserves are readily available to meet debt service payments or to intervene in the foreign exchange market if needed, Dr. Fernando said. He reiterated that the Central Bank maintains a flexible exchange rate, intervening only to mitigate excessive volatility and to build reserves through market purchases.

title: Ravi K calls for  post-EFF IMF program | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 05:06
-     - 18

New Democratic Front MP Ravi Karunanayake yesterday urged the Government to secure a successor to Sri Lanka’s International Monetary Fund (IMF) program, arguing that IMF backing remains crucial despite being unpalatable, as the current arrangement nears its end in March 2027.

Raising questions in Parliament, Karunanayake asked whether, beyond completing the existing IMF program, a successor arrangement had been requested or discussed, and what financing, conditionalities, social protection and debt sustainability steps were being considered.

“We have been saying that going to the IMF is unpalatable, but once you have declared yourself bankrupt, as happened on 12 April 2022, you need to hold hands with the IMF to come out of it,” he said.

“The four-year program is coming to an end in March 2027, so there must be a successor program, and we want to see what it is,” Karunanayake added, describing such a program as necessary to take the country to “a stable tomorrow”.

He questioned whether securing a successor IMF program would better insure Sri Lanka against prolonged external shocks and, if not, what demonstrably more beneficial alternatives could provide comparable financing, credibility and protection. He called on the Government to table its comparative assessment, identify its preferred option and implementation timetable, and report quarterly to Parliament on financing, delivery, outcomes and risks.

Karunanayake framed his call against the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran, which he said began on 20 February, 2026, and threatens Sri Lanka’s recovery through energy, trade and financing shocks.

He sought a quantified Government response on the monthly cumulative additional costs of petroleum, gas, coal, fertiliser, freight and aviation against the pre-war baseline, as well as losses in tourism, exports, overseas employment and investment. He also asked for the effects on growth, inflation, household income, poverty and Government revenue, how these costs were being financed, and who ultimately pays.

On reserves, he asked the Government to disclose usable reserves, restricted reserves, IMF liabilities, import cover and external payments due within 12 months. He further called for three-, six- and 12-month scenarios on the conflict’s duration covering oil prices, financing gaps, reserves and debt service.

Karunanayake also urged that any fuel subsidy be given to the Ceylon Petroleum Corporation (CPC) rather than foreign companies, and asked what strategy, with responsible agencies and deadlines, would diversify energy supply, accelerate renewables, protect migrant workers, secure import markets, attract displaced businesses and preserve balanced diplomatic relations.

Vallibel One PLC has acquired 31.34% of The Fortress Resorts PLC for about Rs. 730 million from two related parties, raising its direct holding in the hotel company to 49.93%.

The diversified conglomerate bought a total of 34,747,249 shares from two concert parties through market transactions on 21 October, 2026, the company said. Concert parties are investors acting together under an agreement or understanding, and in this case all three counterparties to the deal are related.

Vallibel Leisure Ltd. sold 24,417,932 shares, or 22.02% of The Fortress Resorts’ issued ordinary shares, for about Rs. 513 million, while Dhammika Perera sold 10,329,317 shares, or 9.32%, for about Rs. 217 million. Both blocks were sold at Rs. 21 per share.

The purchase lifts Vallibel One’s direct stake from 18.59% to 49.93%. Together with the existing holdings of its subsidiaries L B Finance PLC and Royal Ceramics Lanka PLC, the group’s shareholding in The Fortress Resorts now stands at 53.89%.

Fortress Resorts reported net assets of Rs. 19.84 per share as of end-June 2026. MJF Holdings was the single largest shareholder at that date with a 25.81% stake, followed by Vallibel Leisure (22.02%), Vallibel One (18.59%) and Dhammika Perera (9.32%) and LB Finance (3.65%).

title: Oil reaches six-month high, tops $ 112 on Mideast tensions | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 04:56
-     - 18

Oil prices hit their highest since May yesterday after Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthi movement attacked targets in Saudi Arabia, deepening fears of supply disruption.

Brent crude rose 3.08% to $ 112.17 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) climbed to $ 99.83.

The Houthi attacks, which hit an oil field and a civilian airport, killed at least three people. The US moved to withdraw some diplomatic personnel and their families from Saudi Arabia and other Middle East missions amid fears of further escalation, while reports of explosions in southern Iran and continuing threats to shipping around the Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy shipments, added to market jitters.

The surge has revived concerns over fuel costs and inflation in oil-importing countries, including Sri Lanka, though the impact on domestic fuel prices will depend on international market trends, procurement costs and local pricing decisions.

title: CoPF reviews procurement delays, new Procurement Act and $ 4.5 m digitalisation grant | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 04:46
-     - 17

The Committee on Public Finance (CoPF) has reviewed measures to streamline public procurement process, including progress on a new Procurement Act, efforts to address delays in essential purchases and plans to expand digital monitoring with a $ 4.5 million World Bank grant.

The matters were discussed when the Committee met in Parliament on Tuesday (20) under the Chairmanship of MP Dr. Harsha de Silva.

Discussions on the existing procurement framework focused on delays in purchasing goods and services, registration bottlenecks, shortcomings in the legal framework and challenges in adopting digital systems. Particular attention was paid to expediting the procurement of medicines and other essential goods.

The Committee also considered increasing the financial limits of procurement committees to speed up decisions, introducing long-term framework agreements for recurring purchases and developing sector-specific procurement guidelines.

It also highlighted the need to streamline drug registration procedures over the longer term to minimise delays and improve market competitiveness.

The Committee reviewed the progress of the Procurement Management Information System (PROMIS), which is being implemented to digitise public procurement activities. The system is currently used to monitor procurement processes across 394 active procurement units, including 19 Ministries, with plans to extend coverage to Provincial Councils and all Government Departments by 2027.

The meeting was also briefed on delays in implementing PROMIS and the need to terminate the agreement with the previous contractor. The technical evaluation for selecting a new developer has been completed and forwarded to the World Bank for approval. A $ 4.5 million grant from the Bank is expected to support implementation of the system.

Progress in drafting a new Procurement Act to provide a legal framework for existing procurement guidelines and circulars and streamline the overall process was also discussed.

In addition, issues raised included aligning the draft legislation with the Constitution, delays in obtaining observations from relevant ministries and State institutions, and challenges encountered during revisions to the draft.

The Committee also considered strengthening transparency in public contracts through the disclosure of beneficial ownership information relating to procurement contracts and winning companies, including whether any had previously been blacklisted. Streamlining the appeals process was another area of focus.

Members stressed the importance of better coordination among relevant institutions to minimise administrative and technical obstacles and ensure the efficient use of public funds.

Separately, the Committee approved a proposal submitted under the Public Debt Management Act No. 33 of 2024 and Supplementary Estimate No. 06 for 2026, relating to the loan scheme for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs). Officials said priority would be given to applicants already on the waiting list.

The meeting was attended by Deputy Ministers Chathuranga Abeysinghe and Nishantha Jayaweera, along with MPs Ravi Karunanayake, Nimal Palihena, Rhashana Rajakaruna, Wijesiri Basnayake, Chitral Fernando, Thilina Samarakoon, Ajith Agalakada, Sunil Rajapaksa, Champika Hettiarachchi and Lakmali Hemachandra.

title: Industrial Asphalts disputes auditor’s disclaimer that led to Watch List move | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 04:45
-     - 27

Industrial Asphalts (Ceylon) PLC’s Board has rejected its external auditor’s disclaimer of opinion on the company’s financial statements for the year ended 31 March, 2026. The disclaimer led to the company’s securities being transferred to the Colombo Stock Exchange (CSE) Watch List with effect from 20 October, 2026, the company said yesterday.

This is the company’s second Watch List transfer in under two months. It was first placed on the Watch List on 7 September, 2026 for failing to submit its Annual Report for the year ended 31 March, 2026. It was moved out on 13 October, 2026 after the report was submitted, only to return a week later because of the auditor’s disclaimer.

The first transfer stalled a mandatory offer for the company. Under the CSE Listing Rules, Directors of a company on the Watch List may not transact in its shares without explicit prior approval from the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC). 

On 11 September, 2026, the SEC informed the offerors, Arcasia Investment and Trading Ltd., and ATX Partners Ltd., that it would not approve the share transfer involving Industrial Asphalts Executive Director Ramanan Govindasamy until the company remedied the non-compliance that led to its Watch List placement. The joint offer closed the next day, 12 September, 2026, with acceptances for 1.88 billion shares, or 50.16% of the company, from two major shareholders, Govindasamy and Srikumar Balasubramaniyam.

The company said the main bases for the disclaimer by external auditor B.R. De Silva & Co. were the fair valuation of its investment property and an advance given to Key Management Personnel (KMP) during the year.

According to the company, the auditor disagreed with the investment property valuation report as at 31 March, 2026, prepared by KPMG Real Estate & Valuation Services Ltd., despite a detailed explanation and written clarification from KPMG. After the Annual Report 2026 was published, KPMG provided a further written clarification that it had clearly set out the methodology, market analysis and principal assumptions used to arrive at the fair value. The Board said the auditor had not stated its reasons for disagreeing.

On the KMP advance, the company said the Board Audit Committee obtained an independent legal opinion from an expert legal firm confirming the validity of the payment, which was subsequently settled in full. The auditor rejected that opinion on the grounds that its internal expert had rejected it. The Board then obtained a second legal opinion, which the company said was consistent with the first.

A third basis for the disclaimer related to deferred tax on the revaluation of investment property. The company said it had followed a policy of recognising the investment property revaluation surplus over the years when arriving at the deferred tax impact, but the auditor took a different view in FY 2025/26.

The Board said it would continue to seek clarification from the auditor on its reasons for disputing the KPMG valuation and the legal opinion, together with the profiles of the internal experts who disputed them. It will also take steps to obtain an independent audit opinion from an audit firm, in line with the CSE Listing Rules, so the company can move out of the Watch List. The AGM date will be notified in due course to take this process forward.

The Board intends to resolve the matters within a maximum of six months, as set out in the CSE Listing Rules. If they are not resolved within six months of the Watch List transfer, trading in the company’s securities will be suspended. If the suspension continues for more than 12 months, the CSE’s Board of Directors will delist the securities.

title: Prison population falls 12%; Govt. moves to speed up Analyst’s reports | Daily FT
summary:

Justice Minister Harshana Nanayakkara

Justice Minister Harshana Nanayakkara told Parliament yesterday the prison population fell by 5,068, or 12%, between July and September following measures to ease overcrowding, as the Government moves to clear delays in Government Analyst’s reports.

The number of inmates declined from 41,993 on 1 July to 36,925 by 30 September, he said.

Delays in obtaining Government Analyst’s reports have been identified as one of the main factors behind prison overcrowding. The department issued 1,506 reports in August and September alone after its workforce was strengthened and vacancies filled, Nanayakkara said. Under proposed legislative amendments, the Government Analyst will be required to issue a report within two months of receiving an item for examination.

Further amendments would change the handling of narcotics seized as evidence. Instead of retaining entire packages until court proceedings conclude, authorities will photograph and, where necessary, video-record the substances and inform the relevant Magistrate, who will be empowered to authorise their prompt destruction, subject to conditions imposed by the court.

Nanayakkara said the amendments were intended to ensure the procedures are carried out lawfully, without affecting the fundamental rights of suspects or accused persons, including their right to a fair trial.

SLPP MP Namal Rajapaksa told Parliament yesterday that drugs cannot be eradicated merely by setting targets for arrests.

He said the current approach of setting targets and arresting people to meet them was ineffective, and urged the Government to recognise the limitations of such a strategy.

title: The new currency of leadership | Daily FT
summary:
Friday, 23 October 2026 04:06
-     - 16

As the world becomes more complex, interconnected and uncertain, the qualities required of leaders will continue to evolve. The future belongs to leaders who combine meaningful contribution through purposefulness with meaningful connection through empathy. Such leaders recognise that success is not only about what we achieve, but also about how we influence the lives of others. They understand that flourishing emerges when contribution and connection reinforce one another

Disengagement costs the global economy $8.9 trillion a year, equal to 9 percent of the world’s GDP. People are connected through technology around the clock, yet loneliness and isolation are part of everyday life for millions. Organisations have sophisticated tools for productivity and growth, yet many people are still searching for meaning in their work and lives.

Modern leadership often emphasises one of two priorities. Some leaders focus primarily on achieving goals, driving performance and delivering results. Others place greater emphasis on understanding people, creating engagement and building relationships. Both are important. Yet neither is sufficient on its own. Human flourishing requires both meaningful contribution and meaningful connection.

It is this shared conviction that has brought together Purposeful Leadership and Empathy Everywhere. While emerging from different traditions and experiences, both recognise that flourishing individuals, organisations and societies are built when people are able to contribute meaningfully and connect meaningfully.

Purpose helps us contribute meaningfully. Empathy helps us connect meaningfully. Flourishing requires both.

Going beyond goals

Many leadership models begin with targets, objectives and desired outcomes. While goals are important, they are not the deepest source of motivation or meaning. Purposeful Leadership begins by asking a more fundamental set of questions: Why does this goal matter? What contribution does it make? How does it support the flourishing of life?

A sales target, market expansion or strategic initiative may be impressive in itself. Yet its true significance lies in the value it creates for people and society. When leaders understand the deeper purpose behind goals, they often find greater commitment, resilience and clarity in pursuing them.

Goals are meaningful when they serve a purpose.

Going beyond superficial understanding

Likewise, many leaders believe they understand people because they understand job descriptions, qualifications, personality profiles or demographic characteristics. While such information has value, it only provides a partial picture of the human experience.

Empathy Everywhere invites leaders to look past labels and categories and step into people’s reality: their hopes, fears, aspirations, challenges and sense of belonging. Behind every performance indicator and organisational chart sits a person with a story.

Knowing someone is not the same as understanding them, and understanding people begins with listening to them. The challenge for leaders today is to understand two things well: the purpose of their work and the people they serve.

Purposefulness: A lifelong journey of meaningful contribution

Purposefulness is often misunderstood as finding a single, fixed purpose that remains unchanged throughout life. My own experience and doctoral research suggest something different.

Purposefulness is not about having all the answers. It is an ongoing process of seeking a clearer sense of purpose, acting on our convictions, reflecting on our experiences, gaining new insights and refining our actions. Each cycle teaches us something about ourselves, others and the world around us. As we act, we learn. As we learn, our understanding deepens. As our understanding deepens, our purpose becomes clearer and our actions more purposeful. Purposefulness is therefore not a destination, but a continuous journey of clearer purpose, purposeful action, reflection, insight and growth.

Within the Purposeful Leadership framework, flourishing is viewed through nine interconnected spheres of life: spiritual, emotional, relational, intellectual, physical, financial, temporal, social and ecological. Purposefulness encourages individuals to consider how their actions contribute not only to personal success but also to flourishing across these broader dimensions of life.

The pursuit of purpose is therefore not a destination. It is a way of living. It is an intentional commitment to making meaningful contributions while remaining open to learning, growth and refinement throughout life's journey.

When people find meaning in their work and connect their personal purpose to their organisation's purpose, performance follows. Employees who feel connected to purpose are far more engaged (50 percent versus 9 percent), far less likely to experience burnout (13 percent versus 38 percent), and significantly less likely to be seeking another job (41 percent versus 68 percent) than those who do not. Organisations that strengthen employees' connection to purpose by just 10 percent also see a 4.4 percent increase in profitability. Having worked with thousands of leaders over three decades, Ranjan believes purposefulness helps people stay longer, work smarter, contribute more and grow faster.

Mimi’s experience echoes this. Her purpose found her through connection. As she writes in her upcoming book The Connection Prescription (Out 2027): “Start with empathy again and again, and your purpose will find you.”

Empathy: A pathway to meaningful connection

At its simplest, empathy is the ability to recognise and respond to the reality or viewpoint of another. It is the skill of understanding the experiences of the people we live and work with. Neuroscience tells us that empathy is a skill set we are born with, not a personality trait reserved for a few. Far from being a soft attribute, empathy is a measurable human skill with measurable organisational outcomes. Like any skill, it can be practised, strengthened and applied to create measurable results."

Listening is the backbone of all empathy, and curiosity is the backbone of all listening. Empathy asks us to set our assumptions aside, ask questions and stay curious about how another person experiences their work and their world. If we don’t ask, how will we ever know?

When people are heard and understood, performance follows. They are 48 percent more innovative, 64 percent more engaged and 17 percent more efficient, and they drive 23 percent higher profits. Having worked with over twenty thousand people, Mimi believes listening alone may solve up to 80 percent of the disconnection issues in the workplace.

This is the survival of the connected. Leaders who listen are leaders of longevity.

Where purposefulness and empathy meet

Human flourishing can emerge through many pathways. Purposefulness creates enormous value by helping people find meaning, direction and contribution, leading to higher engagement, lower burnout, stronger retention and higher profitability. Empathy creates enormous value by helping people build understanding, belonging and connection, leading to higher engagement, greater innovation, improved efficiency and higher profitability. Although they travel different paths, both demonstrate the powerful relationship between human flourishing and organisational success.

What is particularly interesting is that the two approaches often lead to remarkably similar outcomes through different mechanisms: 

Purpose helps people understand why their work matters. Empathy helps people feel that they matter. 

Purpose creates alignment between personal aspirations and organisational contribution. Empathy creates connection between individual experiences and collective success. 

One strengthens meaningful contribution; the other strengthens meaningful connection.

Together they offer an even richer perspective on flourishing. Purposefulness encourages us to ask, “How can I contribute meaningfully?” Empathy encourages us to ask, “How can I connect meaningfully?” Both move people beyond self-interest towards a greater concern for others, and both can be consciously developed throughout life. In many ways, each contains elements of the other. Purposefulness naturally encourages consideration of others, while empathy naturally inspires contribution to others. Whether pursued independently or in combination, both help individuals, organisations and societies flourish. When meaningful contribution and meaningful connection reinforce one another, that potential becomes even greater.

How empathy enriches purposefulness

While purposefulness provides meaningful direction and energy, empathy enhances the quality and relevance of that direction and energy. Empathy begins with ourselves. Self-empathy helps us understand our own needs, motives and limits, and our interactions with others often reveal what we might otherwise overlook. Empathy helps us understand human needs accurately. It allows us to anticipate the consequences of our decisions. It keeps us grounded in reality. Most importantly, it helps ensure our contributions benefit the people we seek to serve.

A purposeful individual may ask, “What contribution should I make?” Empathy encourages an equally important question: “How is that contribution experienced by others?” Mimi’s first question to leaders is always the same: Have you actually asked your team? 

Ranjan’s doctoral research identified four recurring complexities associated with purposeful living and leadership. Empathy has the potential to help individuals navigate each of these complexities more effectively.

Cognitive complexity arises because decisions about purpose rarely involve a single perspective. Listening to a range of voices broadens understanding and brings competing interpretations of reality into view.

Psychosocial complexity emerges because purpose unfolds within relationships and communities. Listening creates environments where people are valued enough to be heard, and relationships grow healthier as a result.

Practical complexity reflects the challenge of translating purpose into everyday realities. Empathy helps us understand what people can realistically embrace and sustain within organisational and social constraints.

Contextual complexity arises because people operate within diverse cultures, systems and environments. Empathy encourages sensitivity to those differences and reduces the likelihood of imposing one-size-fits-all solutions.

 An empathetic approach enriches purposefulness. It keeps purpose grounded in people’s reality and responsive to their lives.

How purposefulness enriches empathy

 The relationship works in both directions.

Just as empathy enriches purposefulness, purposefulness also enriches empathy.

Empathy allows us to understand people. Mimi teaches acknowledgement over action: listen first, recognise what you have heard, and then decide how to respond. Stop. Recognise. Progress. Understanding alone does not automatically create positive impact, and this is where purposefulness guides what comes next.

Purposefulness adds direction, meaning, values, commitment and aspiration.

It encourages us to ask: What should we do with what we have understood? How can understanding lead to positive change? How can connection contribute to flourishing?

Purposefulness transforms empathy from understanding into action. It helps leaders convert insight into action and compassion into meaningful outcomes.

Empathy helps us recognise what matters to people. Purposefulness helps us decide how to respond in ways that generate value and contribute to flourishing.

A purposeful approach enriches empathy. It helps empathy become more impactful.

A new model for flourishing leadership

The leadership challenges of the future may require a deeper integration of purposefulness and empathy than has traditionally been recognised.

Purposefulness asks: How should I conduct myself for the flourishing of life?

Empathy asks: Whom am I serving and how do they experience the world?

Together these questions help leaders understand themselves and the people around them. They encourage leaders to contribute meaningfully and connect authentically. They support flourishing organisations where performance and humanity grow together.

Such leaders are not only capable of achieving results. They are capable of building environments where people can grow, belong and contribute. They strengthen organisations while also strengthening communities and society.

Perhaps the most powerful insight emerging from this partnership is that empathy helps purposefulness become wiser, while purposefulness helps empathy become more impactful.

Together they create the conditions for meaningful contribution, meaningful connection and human flourishing.

Putting purposefulness and empathy into practice

The integration of purposefulness and empathy is not merely a philosophy; it is a set of practices that leaders can cultivate every day. Here are a few practical ways to strengthen both meaningful contribution and meaningful connection.

The Purpose Conversation: Take time to understand what matters most to the people you lead. What strengths do they most enjoy using to create value? What contribution do they hope to make? What gives them a sense of meaning? 

Empathy often reveals purpose.

Ask Why, Then Ask Who: Before making an important decision, ask: Why does this matter? Then ask: Who will be affected, and how will they experience it?

Ask Before Deciding: Before making an important decision, ask your people. Listen not only for their opinions, but also for what gives them meaning, energy and purpose.

Ask Those Who Matter Most: When you revisit an important decision, invite the people affected to help shape its refinement. 

Purpose becomes more meaningful when those impacted by it have a voice in it.

The Double Ask: When someone tells you what they enjoy doing, ask again. 

The first answer is often about what people do. The second answer often reveals the why: the motivations, values, contribution - the seeds of purpose itself.

The Acknowledgement Pause: Before responding, pause and reflect back what you heard to ensure you have understood correctly.

Be Fully Present: Put the phone down and give people your attention. Listening requires authenticity. 

It requires presence. It requires you, fully.

As Ranjan often reminds leaders, meaningful change rarely comes from a single insight. It comes from persistent practice, reflection, learning and refinement over time. And as Mimi teaches leaders around the world, “practice creates permanence.” Together, these principles remind us that flourishing leadership is built one conversation, one action and one practice at a time.

Conclusion: Meaningful contribution, meaningful connection

As the world becomes more complex, interconnected and uncertain, the qualities required of leaders will continue to evolve.

The future belongs to leaders who combine meaningful contribution through purposefulness with meaningful connection through empathy.

Such leaders recognise that success is not only about what we achieve, but also about how we influence the lives of others. They understand that flourishing emerges when contribution and connection reinforce one another.

When purposefulness guides our contribution, and empathy shapes our connection, we move closer to what every person, organisation and society seeks: the flourishing of life. Start with empathy, and purpose will follow.
